run.topic: best web-design / UI component libraries & animation techniques to de-stale my sites

Some design blogs (Josh Comeau, Smashing, NN/g, web.dev) were egress-blocked (connect_rejected) in this session; the visual-polish facet was re-anchored to official design-token source files (Tailwind theme.css, Open Props) that were actually retrieved. No quotes were fabricated.

findings.claim: Adopt shadcn/ui as your base component system — its CLI copies modern, accessible components (Radix + Tailwind) into your repo so you own and freely restyle the code, instead of fighting a black-box npm design system.
findings.evidence_quote: A set of beautifully designed components that you can customize, extend, and build on. Start here then make it your own. Open Source. Open Code.

payload.command: npx shadcn@latest init && npx shadcn@latest add button card dialog input
payload.note: Works with Tailwind v3. Components land in components/ui and are yours to restyle.

findings.claim: Build dropdowns, dialogs, tooltips and comboboxes on Radix Primitives, which supplies accessibility (ARIA, focus management, keyboard nav) unstyled so you apply your own Tailwind — adopt it incrementally as the base layer of your design system.
findings.evidence_quote: Radix Primitives is a low-level UI component library with a focus on accessibility, customization and developer experience. You can use these components either as the base layer of your design system, or adopt them incrementally.

payload.note: shadcn/ui already sits on Radix; adding Radix directly is for primitives shadcn doesn't cover.

findings.claim: For lightweight interactive primitives (menus, dialogs, comboboxes, transitions) without the full shadcn/Radix stack, add Headless UI — it's from the Tailwind team and integrates natively with Tailwind, so it drops in with almost no setup.
findings.evidence_quote: A set of completely unstyled, fully accessible UI components for React, designed to integrate beautifully with Tailwind CSS.

payload.note: Lowest-friction way to replace hand-rolled menus/modals with accessible ones.

findings.claim: If you want pre-styled speed over assembly, consider HeroUI (formerly NextUI): a batteries-included, beautiful-by-default, Tailwind-native React library — but its current version is built on Tailwind v4.0, so adopting it means migrating your sites off Tailwind v3.
findings.evidence_quote: 🚀 Beautiful and modern React UI library built with Tailwind CSS 4.0.

payload.note: Effort=involved: requires a Tailwind v3→v4 migration first. Weigh against staying on shadcn (v3-compatible).

findings.claim: Fix the 'plain/stale' look on landing and marketing pages by layering in motion-rich components from Magic UI (and sibling Aceternity UI) — animated hero/section effects that install via the same shadcn-style CLI and drop into your Next+Tailwind setup.

payload.note: Use sparingly on hero sections; over-animation reads as busy (see f-12).

findings.claim: Standardize your component workflow around the shadcn CLI (`npx shadcn add ...`): shadcn/ui, Magic UI and Aceternity all distribute through this same add-to-your-app mechanism, so package the 'add + wire in a component' procedure as a reusable skill.

payload.skill_md:
---
name: add-ui-component
description: Add and wire in a UI component from a shadcn-compatible registry (shadcn/ui, Magic UI, Aceternity). Use when the user wants to drop in a button, dialog, animated hero, marquee, or other prebuilt component into a Next.js + Tailwind project.
allowed-tools: Bash(npx shadcn *), Read, Edit
---

# Add a UI component

1. Confirm the registry + component name (shadcn/ui default, or a full URL for Magic UI / Aceternity).
2. Run `npx shadcn@latest add <name-or-url>`.
3. Import it where needed and wire props; keep styling in Tailwind classes so it matches the site's tokens.
4. Check it against prefers-reduced-motion if it animates.

findings.claim: Adopt Motion (formerly Framer Motion) as your default for React micro-motion — declarative entrances, hover/tap gestures, and layout transitions. It's TypeScript-native and GPU-accelerated, so it fits your Next 15 + TS UI cleanly.

source.title: Motion — animation library for JS, React and Vue
source.author: Motion (motiondivision)

findings.evidence_quote: Power of JavaScript combined with native browser APIs for 120fps, GPU-accelerated animations.

payload.note: import { motion } from "motion/react"; then <motion.div animate={{ x: 100 }} />. Pair with f-11/f-12 for tasteful defaults.

findings.claim: For page/route feel, enable View Transitions in Next.js and wrap shared elements (a grid thumbnail that becomes a hero) in <ViewTransition> with a matching name — the browser animates route changes automatically, and unsupported browsers just navigate normally.
findings.evidence_quote: You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions.

payload.note: Then wrap shared elements in <ViewTransition name="...">. Progressive: no-support = normal nav.

findings.claim: Replace scroll-event listeners / IntersectionObserver 'reveal on scroll' JS with native CSS animation-timeline: view() (scroll-triggered) or scroll() (scroll-linked). Zero JavaScript, so scroll animations stop competing for the main thread and won't jank your marketing pages.
findings.evidence_quote: Any time you rely on the main thread to render effects with JavaScript, you run the risk of blocking the main thread, which can lead to an unresponsive page and a bad user experience

payload.note: Pair with f-10 feature-detection for Firefox fallback.

findings.claim: Treat scroll-driven animations as progressive enhancement: gate the CSS behind @supports (animation-timeline: view()) so browsers that lack support (notably Firefox stable) fall back to fully-readable static content instead of breaking.

payload.diff:
+ - Scroll-driven CSS animations are progressive enhancement: always gate them behind
+   `@supports (animation-timeline: view())` so unsupported browsers get readable static content.

findings.claim: Always wrap non-essential motion in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) and tone it down — swap scaling/sliding for a gentle opacity dissolve, or drop durations to 0. Large scaling/panning can physically trigger discomfort, so this is a baseline accessibility must.
findings.evidence_quote: Animations such as scaling or panning large objects can be vestibular motion triggers.

payload.diff:
+ - All non-essential motion must be wrapped in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`
+   (reduce to an opacity fade or 0ms). Never ship scaling/panning motion without it.

findings.claim: Make motion subtle and quick so it reads as 'considered', not 'busy': small travel (~60px), short durations (exits ~150ms, enters ~200–400ms), and make exits faster than entrances. That fast-out/gentle-in asymmetry separates tasteful motion from over-animated jank.
findings.evidence_quote: Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it.

payload.diff:
+ - Motion defaults: travel ≤ ~60px; enters 200–400ms, exits ~150ms (exits faster than enters).
+   Prefer opacity+small-translate over scale. If it feels 'busy', it's too much.

findings.claim: Stop hand-picking a font-size per element. Commit to one type scale where every step pairs with a matching line-height (as Tailwind's own theme defines it) and use only those steps — ad-hoc type sizing is the single biggest tell of a generic, AI-generated page.

payload.diff:
+ - Type: use only the defined scale (text-sm/base/lg/xl/2xl…) with its paired line-height.
+   No ad-hoc font sizes. Ad-hoc sizing is the #1 tell of a generic page.

findings.claim: Drive all padding, margin and gap from one spacing base unit (Tailwind's is 0.25rem / 4px) instead of ad-hoc pixel values, so vertical rhythm and gaps snap to a consistent grid across every section rather than drifting.

payload.diff: + - Spacing: every padding/margin/gap comes from the 4px spacing scale. No ad-hoc px values.

findings.claim: Replace flat single box-shadows with a multi-layer shadow — several stacked shadow lines sharing one shadow-color and graduated opacity — and store them as reusable tokens (shadow-1…6) so elevation reads as deliberate depth, not a default drop shadow.

payload.note: Or copy the layered-shadow tokens into your Tailwind theme extend.boxShadow.

findings.claim: Don't reuse light-mode shadows in dark mode. Under prefers-color-scheme: dark, shift the shadow color much darker and raise its strength (Open Props jumps strength from ~1% to 25%), or elevation and cards visually flatten on dark surfaces.

payload.diff: + - Dark mode: never reuse light shadows — darken shadow-color and raise strength, or cards flatten.

findings.claim: Define a small set of named easing tokens (custom cubic-beziers — an ease-out for entering elements) and reference them in every transition, instead of leaving each hover/press on the browser default ease. Shared, intentional easing makes motion feel considered.

payload.diff: + - Easing: reference named easing tokens (e.g. --ease-out-5) in transitions; no default ease.

findings.claim: When you use a gradient, reach for a rich multi-stop blend (Open Props gradients chain 6–8 hand-tuned colors) rather than a flat two-color linear-gradient, and save it as a token so it's reused consistently — flat 2-stop gradients are a classic generic-template signal.

payload.change: Define a multi-stop gradient token; reuse it instead of ad-hoc 2-color gradients.
